title: Remember Me
hookLine: remember Me, I will remember you, be grateful and don't deny (2:152)

lines: A PROMISE THAT TAKES A LONG TIME.
cards: Some promises take a long time to arrive. A grandmother saves for a grandchild's education, and the grandchild graduates years after she's gone. A letter mailed long ago turns up in the right hands at last.

Three days ago, Ibrahim and Isma'il prayed for a messenger who would come long after them. Today al-Baqarah reaches back to that prayer, says it's been answered, and asks one thing in return. Today: remember Me.

teach.b: Put two verses side by side. Verse one hundred twenty-nine, Ibrahim's prayer: send them a messenger from among them, who will recite Your verses, teach the book and wisdom, and purify them.

Verse one hundred fifty-one, God speaking to the first Muslims: We have sent among you a messenger from among you, who recites Our verses to you, purifies you, teaches you the book and wisdom, and teaches you what you did not know.
Everything Ibrahim asked for, and one thing more, twenty-two verses apart. Commentators notice the order changes too: in the answer, purifying comes before teaching.
Then the very next verse, in Pickthall's words: “Therefore remember Me, I will remember you.” Therefore: because the prayer was answered, because the gift arrived. Al-Baqarah doesn't ask for payment.
It asks for remembrance, and then for gratitude: give thanks to Me, and don't deny Me.

teach.h: REMEMBRANCE AND GRATITUDE, SIDE BY SIDE
teach.b: Remembrance and gratitude side by side, like one act seen from two angles. And it's a two-way promise: you remember; you are remembered.
A hadith qudsi in Bukhari adds one detail: whoever remembers God in a gathering, God remembers them in a better gathering. Last year you learned dhikr, the practice of remembering.
Here the Qur'an puts it right after a gift long in coming. The community was remembered first, in a prayer said over stones long before.
It remembers back, and is remembered back.

how: Muslims practice dhikr, repeating short phrases such as subhan Allah, alhamdulillah and Allahu akbar after prayer and through the day, often counting on the fingers or on prayer beads.

o: a prayer asking God not to forget the dead
remember God, and be remembered; give thanks
Ibrahim's last words to his son at the Kaaba

games.q: the prayer and its answer — tap the pairs.
p: We have sent among you a messenger

s: 2:151 answers Ibrahim's prayer in 2:129 with exactly the same list
everything he asked for, in a new order, plus one more: teaching what they did not know.
the verse asks for payment in return for the messenger
it asks for remembrance and gratitude.
in Ibrahim's prayer it came after; the answer moves it ahead.

games.q: a gift prayed for long ago has arrived. what does al-Baqarah ask of you next?
o: remember Me, I will remember you; be grateful.
games.why: therefore remember Me: the request comes right after the gift, and it's a two-way promise.

practice: If you pray, choose one short phrase you know, subhan Allah, alhamdulillah or Allahu akbar, and say it softly with the breath, counting on your fingers if you like.
If you don't, bring back one person who remembered you when you needed it, and let their name return with each breath, unhurried.

wordCard.voice: Remember Me. Al-Baqarah's request, right after the answer to Ibrahim's prayer: remember Me, I will remember you; be grateful, and don't deny. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: so remember Me, I will remember you (2:152); the fa, therefore, ties it to the verse before.

carryVoice: Your line: remembered back. Remembering is how a gift that big is received. That's day three hundred forty-seven.

sources.q: Therefore remember Me, I will remember you.

sources.ref: Qur'an 2:129 and 2:151 (the prayer for a messenger and its answer)
Sahih al-Bukhari 7405 (hadith qudsi: remembered in a better gathering)
